sections.readable_text: A particle [MATH: P] moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin [MATH: O.] Its velocity [MATH: v\,\textrm{m/s}] is given by [MATH: v(t) =3t^2-2t,] where [MATH: t] is the time in seconds. Calculate the total distance traveled by [MATH: P] in the interval [MATH: \dfrac{2}{3}\leq t\leq 1 .]

sections.normalized_html:
To find the total distance traveled, we first need to find the points where the particle changes its direction, which can only occur when the velocity is zero. Solving [MATH: v(t) = 0,] we get [MATH: \eqalign{ v(t) &= 0 \ 3t^2 - 2t&= 0 \ t(3t -2) & = 0 \ t & =0, \dfrac{2}{3} . }]

The graph of the velocity [MATH: v(t)] is given below:

Notice that in the interval [MATH: \dfrac{2}{3} \leq t\leq 1,] the graph of [MATH: v(t)] doesn't cross the [MATH: t]-axis. Therefore, we don't need to split up the distance integral.

In the interval [MATH: \dfrac{2}{3} \leq t\leq 1,] we have [MATH: v(t)\geq 0.] Therefore, [MATH: |v(t)| = v(t) = 3t^2-2t.]

We can now calculate the total distance traveled, as follows:

[MATH: \eqalign{ d&=\int_{2/3}^1 |v(t)| \, dt\[5pt] &=\int_{2/3}^{1} \left(3t^2-2t \right)\,\textrm{d}t\[5pt] &=\Big.\left(t^3-t^2 \right)\Big|_{2/3}^{1}\[5pt] &=\left(1^3-1^2 \right)-\left( \left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^3-\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^2\right)\[5pt] &=\dfrac{4}{9}-\dfrac{8}{27}\[5pt] &=\dfrac{4}{27} }]

Therefore, the particle travels a total distance of [MATH: \dfrac{4}{27}\,\textrm m] in the time interval [MATH: \dfrac{2}{3}\leq t\leq 1.]

A particle [MATH: P] moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin [MATH: O.] Its displacement [MATH: s\,\textrm{cm}] is given by

[MATH: s(t) =2t^3-6t^2+4,]
where [MATH: t] is the time, in seconds. Calculate the total distance traveled by [MATH: P] in the interval [MATH: 0\leq t\leq 4 .]

sections.normalized_html:
The displacement [MATH: s(t)] is given by [MATH: s(t) =2t^3-6t^2+4.] The velocity [MATH: v(t)] is obtained by differentiating [MATH: s(t).] This gives [MATH: \eqalign{ v(t)&=\dfrac{\textrm{d}s}{\textrm{d}t}=6t^2-12t. }]

To find the total distance traveled, we need to find the points where the velocity changes direction. This occurs when the velocity is zero. Solving [MATH: v(t) = 0,] we get [MATH: \eqalign{ 6t^2-12t &= 0 \ 6t(t -2) & = 0 \ t & =0,2. }]

A sketch of [MATH: v(t)] is shown below:

Notice that in the interval [MATH: 0\leq t\leq 4,] the curve [MATH: v(t)] crosses the [MATH: t]-axis at [MATH: t=2.] Therefore, total distance traveled [MATH: d] is given by

[MATH: d = \left|s(2) - s(0)| + |s(4) - s(2)\right|.]

We calculate the total distance traveled as follows:

[MATH: d|=|(2(2)^{3} − 6(2)^{2} + 4) − (4)|+|(2(4)^{3} − 6(4)^{2} + 4) − (2(2)^{3} − 6(2)^{2} + 4)|; = 8 + 40; = 48m]

Therefore, the total distance traveled by [MATH: P] in the interval [MATH: 0 \leq t\leq 4] is [MATH: 48\,\textrm{ m}.]

sections.normalized_html:
To find the total distance traveled, we first need to find the points where the particle changes its direction, which can only occur when the velocity is zero. Solving [MATH: v(t) = 0,] we get

[MATH: v(t)|= 0; (1)/(2)t − 1|= 0; (1)/(2)t|= 1; t|= 2.]

A sketch of [MATH: v(t)] is shown below:

Notice that in the interval [MATH: 0\leq t\leq T] for [MATH: T > 2,] the curve [MATH: v(t)] crosses the [MATH: t]-axis at [MATH: t=2.] Therefore, we need to split up the distance integral between the intervals [MATH: 0\leq t\leq 2] and [MATH: 2\leq t\leq T.]

In the interval [MATH: 0 \leq t\leq 2,] we have [MATH: v(t) \lt 0.] Therefore, [MATH: |v(t)| = -v(t) = 1 - \dfrac{1}{2}t.]

Similarly, in the interval [MATH: 2 \leq t \leq T,] we have [MATH: v(t) \gt 0.] Therefore, [MATH: |v(t)| = v(t) = \dfrac{1}{2}t - 1.]

Finally, splitting the integral over the two intervals, we can find an expression for the total distance traveled, as follows:

[MATH: d|= ∫_{0}^{T}|v(t)|dt; = ∫_{0}^{2}|v(t)|dt + ∫_{2}^{T}|v(t)|dt; = ∫_{0}^{2}(1 − (1)/(2)t)dt + ∫_{2}^{T}((1)/(2)t − 1)dt; = (t − (1)/(4)t^{2})|_{0}^{2} + ((1)/(4)t^{2} − t)|_{2}^{T}; = [(2 − (1)/(4)(2)^{2}) − 0] + [((1)/(4)T^{2} − T) − ((1)/(4)(2)^{2} − 2)]; = 1 + (1)/(4)T^{2} − T − (− 1); = (1)/(4)T^{2} − T + 2]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The total distance [MATH: d] traveled by a particle over the time interval [MATH: [t_1,t_2]] is given by

Content:
[MATH: d = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} |v(t)|\,\textrm d t.]

Content:
In other words, we integrate the speed of the particle over the relevant time interval.

Content:
Watch out! We need to integrate the speed [MATH: |v(t)|,] not just the velocity [MATH: v(t).] Integrating the velocity gives us displacement, which is not the same as distance.

Content:
For example, if you take a step forward and then a step backward, your total distance traveled is [MATH: 2] steps, while your displacement is [MATH: 0] steps.

---

Item 2 — Example: Calculating the Total Distance Traveled by a Particle

Example Prompt:
A particle [MATH: P] moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin [MATH: O.] Its velocity [MATH: v\,\textrm{m/s}] is given by [MATH: v(t) =3t^2-2t,] where [MATH: t] is the time in seconds. Calculate the total distance traveled by [MATH: P] in the interval [MATH: \dfrac{2}{3}\leq t\leq 1 .]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
To find the total distance traveled, we first need to find the points where the particle changes its direction, which can only occur when the velocity is zero. Solving [MATH: v(t) = 0,] we get
[MATH: \eqalign{
v(t) &= 0 \
3t^2 - 2t&= 0 \
t(3t -2) & = 0 \
t & =0, \dfrac{2}{3} .
}]

The graph of the velocity [MATH: v(t)] is given below:

[IMG: /graphics/e20372269fde052019afad9992ab801e]

Notice that in the interval [MATH: \dfrac{2}{3} \leq t\leq 1,] the graph of [MATH: v(t)] doesn't cross the [MATH: t]-axis. Therefore, we don't need to split up the distance integral.

In the interval [MATH: \dfrac{2}{3} \leq t\leq 1,] we have [MATH: v(t)\geq 0.] Therefore,
[MATH: |v(t)| = v(t) = 3t^2-2t.]

We can now calculate the total distance traveled, as follows:

[MATH: \eqalign{
d&=\int_{2/3}^1 |v(t)| \, dt\[5pt]
&=\int_{2/3}^{1} \left(3t^2-2t \right)\,\textrm{d}t\[5pt]
&=\Big.\left(t^3-t^2 \right)\Big|_{2/3}^{1}\[5pt]
&=\left(1^3-1^2 \right)-\left( \left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^3-\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^2\right)\[5pt]
&=\dfrac{4}{9}-\dfrac{8}{27}\[5pt]
&=\dfrac{4}{27}
}]

Therefore, the particle travels a total distance of [MATH: \dfrac{4}{27}\,\textrm m] in the time interval [MATH: \dfrac{2}{3}\leq t\leq 1.]

Item 5 — Example: Calculating the Total Distance Traveled by a Particle When It Changes Direction

Example Prompt:
A particle [MATH: P] moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin [MATH: O.] Its displacement [MATH: s\,\textrm{cm}] is given by

[MATH: s(t) =2t^3-6t^2+4,]
where [MATH: t] is the time, in seconds. Calculate the total distance traveled by [MATH: P] in the interval [MATH: 0\leq t\leq 4 .]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The displacement [MATH: s(t)] is given by
[MATH: s(t) =2t^3-6t^2+4.]
The velocity [MATH: v(t)] is obtained by differentiating [MATH: s(t).] This gives
[MATH: \eqalign{
v(t)&=\dfrac{\textrm{d}s}{\textrm{d}t}=6t^2-12t.
}]

To find the total distance traveled, we need to find the points where the velocity changes direction. This occurs when the velocity is zero. Solving [MATH: v(t) = 0,] we get
[MATH: \eqalign{
6t^2-12t &= 0 \
6t(t -2) & = 0 \
t & =0,2.
}]

A sketch of [MATH: v(t)] is shown below:

[IMG: /graphics/12afae1ccf84d653c53e73981d061bd4]

Notice that in the interval [MATH: 0\leq t\leq 4,] the curve [MATH: v(t)] crosses the [MATH: t]-axis at [MATH: t=2.] Therefore, total distance traveled [MATH: d] is given by

[MATH: d = \left|s(2) - s(0)| + |s(4) - s(2)\right|.]

We calculate the total distance traveled as follows:

[MATH: d|=|(2(2)^{3} − 6(2)^{2} + 4) − (4)|+|(2(4)^{3} − 6(4)^{2} + 4) − (2(2)^{3} − 6(2)^{2} + 4)|; = 8 + 40; = 48m]

Therefore, the total distance traveled by [MATH: P] in the interval [MATH: 0 \leq t\leq 4] is [MATH: 48\,\textrm{ m}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
To find the total distance traveled, we first need to find the points where the particle changes its direction, which can only occur when the velocity is zero. Solving [MATH: v(t) = 0,] we get

[MATH: v(t)|= 0; (1)/(2)t − 1|= 0; (1)/(2)t|= 1; t|= 2.]

A sketch of [MATH: v(t)] is shown below:

[IMG: /graphics/0489c64bccb52ed9728b8d0ac517da4e]

Notice that in the interval [MATH: 0\leq t\leq T] for [MATH: T > 2,] the curve [MATH: v(t)] crosses the [MATH: t]-axis at [MATH: t=2.] Therefore, we need to split up the distance integral between the intervals [MATH: 0\leq t\leq 2] and [MATH: 2\leq t\leq T.]

In the interval [MATH: 0 \leq t\leq 2,] we have [MATH: v(t) \lt 0.] Therefore,
[MATH: |v(t)| = -v(t) = 1 - \dfrac{1}{2}t.]

Similarly, in the interval [MATH: 2 \leq t \leq T,] we have [MATH: v(t) \gt 0.] Therefore,
[MATH: |v(t)| = v(t) = \dfrac{1}{2}t - 1.]

Finally, splitting the integral over the two intervals, we can find an expression for the total distance traveled, as follows:

[MATH: d|= ∫_{0}^{T}|v(t)|dt; = ∫_{0}^{2}|v(t)|dt + ∫_{2}^{T}|v(t)|dt; = ∫_{0}^{2}(1 − (1)/(2)t)dt + ∫_{2}^{T}((1)/(2)t − 1)dt; = (t − (1)/(4)t^{2})|_{0}^{2} + ((1)/(4)t^{2} − t)|_{2}^{T}; = [(2 − (1)/(4)(2)^{2}) − 0] + [((1)/(4)T^{2} − T) − ((1)/(4)(2)^{2} − 2)]; = 1 + (1)/(4)T^{2} − T − (− 1); = (1)/(4)T^{2} − T + 2]
